claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy with B2 ordering.
The initial alloy has a fine lamellar microstructure.
Aging at approximately 500–700 °C evolves local chemical order within the B2 phase.
Intermediate aging produces an LCO state that maximizes the APB energy in B2.
LCO evolution produces coherent, high-energy FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Dislocations entering ordered B2 domains must create anti-phase boundaries.
Hard B2 domains and B2 precipitates can pin dislocation motion in an FCC/B2 eutectic HEA.
High Ti content in ordered gamma-prime precipitates increases APB energy.
The high-Ti gamma-prime result is mechanistically analogous to LCO-induced APB strengthening in the B2 phase of the proposed HEA.
Increased APB energy raises the barrier to dislocation transmission across FCC/B2 interfaces.
The transmission barrier causes dislocation pile-up at phase boundaries and brittle fracture.
At higher temperatures, thermal activation permits dislocations to cross-slip or overcome the APB barrier.
Higher-temperature exposure can disorder the LCOs, lower APB energy, and restore ductility.
The alloy should exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile response as aging temperature increases.
Impurity-segregation and simple grain-coarsening models predict monotonic degradation or recovery rather than a transient brittle peak.

The embrittlement regime is the temperature interval in which LCOs remain stable and APB energy is maximized, excluding conditions dominated by grain-boundary fracture or complete B2 dissolution/disordering.
Warren-Cowley parameters can be used to track B2-related chemical ordering.
APB energy can be derived from the measured dislocation splitting width.
Higher APB energy should appear as wider dislocation splitting in the peak-embrittlement sample.
Phase-boundary dislocation pile-ups and transgranular fracture would distinguish the proposed mechanism from grain-boundary embrittlement, which would instead produce intergranular fracture.
